title: Functions
summary: Name a reusable task, give it inputs, and **return** a result.
refresher: A C++ **function** writes its **return type** before its name and gives every **parameter** a type. For example, `int square(int n)` accepts an integer and returns an integer. In Coding Tutor practice, keep the starter function line exactly as given, then write your logic inside it.

sections.title: Read the function signature
sections.summary: Identify the **return type**, **function** name, and typed **parameters**.

blocks.body: A **function** gives a name to a reusable task. Its **parameters** receive **input** values, and `return` sends a result back to the caller. In C++, the function also states the type of each input and the type of its result.

blocks.caption: Before real syntax, learn the shape: a **function** has a name, inputs, a body, and sometimes a returned result. The examples after this show the exact syntax.
blocks.code:
function name(parameters):
    body that does the job
    return the result

call function name(arguments)

blocks.caption: See arguments enter a function, a local variable appear, and return send the answer back.

blocks.body: Read `int larger(int a, int b)` from left to right: the **function** returns an `int`, its name is `larger`, and it receives two **integer** **parameters**. A call such as `larger(7, 4)` fills those parameters and waits for the returned answer.

blocks.title: Keep the starter shape
blocks.body: The practice runner calls the exact **function** from the starter. If the starter says `long long temperatureAboveThreshold(std::vector<long long> readings, long long threshold)`, keep that line. Do not wrap it in a `class Solution`, rename it, or change `long long` to `int`.

blocks.title: C++ types are the main difference from Python here
blocks.body: Python writes `def square(n):`. C++ writes `int square(int n)`. Both name the **function** and its **input**, but C++ also states that the input and result are **integers**.

blocks.caption: The **arguments** 7 and 4 fill a and b. The **function** returns 7, and main prints it.

sections.title: Match arguments to typed parameters
sections.summary: A call fills **parameters** by position, and C++ checks the declared types.

blocks.body: When a C++ **function** is called, the first **argument** fills the first **parameter**, the second fills the second, and so on. The names inside the function do not have to match the caller names, but the types and order still matter.

blocks.caption: The call sends `7` into `score` and `3` into `bonus`. The returned result is a number, not printed text.

blocks.title: Read the comma list slowly
blocks.body: For `int addBonus(int score, int bonus)`, both inputs are integers. If the runner sends a vector or a string, the signature must say so.

blocks.prompt: In `int addBonus(int score, int bonus)`, what does the second argument fill?
blocks.why: Arguments fill parameters by position, so `3` fills the second parameter, `bonus`.

sections.title: Return the promised value
sections.summary: Use **return** in non-void **functions** and keep Coding Tutor starter shapes intact.

blocks.caption: A non-void **function** must use **return** to send its answer back.
For Coding Tutor C++ practice, keep the top-level **function** the runner expects.

blocks.body: The first version calculates a **value** but throws it away. The corrected version returns the result to the line that called the **function**. Make sure every possible path in a non-void function returns the promised type.

blocks.title: Return the promised result
blocks.body: If a **function** begins with a type such as `int` or `double`, the caller expects a result of that type. Use `return` on every possible path. A `void` function performs work without returning a **value**.

sections.title: Check every branch that can return
sections.summary: A non-void **function** should have a result for each possible path.

blocks.body: Conditionals inside a **function** create multiple paths. Trace one input for each path and ask what value reaches `return`.

blocks.caption: This bug appears when one branch returns but the other path falls through.

blocks.prompt: Why is the corrected version safer?
choices: Each path gives back an int
blocks.why: The function promises an integer result, and now both the positive and non-positive paths return one.

blocks.title: Functions checklist
items: Keep the practice starter **function** name and types.
**Return** the promised type on every path.
Use void only when no result is needed.

call-01.title: Definition is not execution
call-01.body: A function or method body waits until code calls it.
call-01.notice: Find the actual call before expecting the body to run.
call-01.mistake: Do not count a function body just because it appears above the output line.

print-not-return-01.title: Printing is not returning
print-not-return-01.body: Printing shows a value to the person. Returning hands a value back to the program.
print-not-return-01.notice: Check whether the function has a return value or only output side effects.
print-not-return-01.mistake: Do not store the result of a no-return function and expect a useful value instead of nothing from void.

return-value-01.title: Returned values replace the call
return-value-01.body: A function call with a return value can be used inside a larger expression.
return-value-01.notice: Evaluate each call, replace it with its returned value, then finish the expression.
return-value-01.mistake: Do not ignore the returned value when the next line uses it.

return-stops-01.title: Return exits immediately
return-stops-01.body: Once a return statement runs, the rest of that function call is over.
return-stops-01.notice: After an early return, skip later lines in the same function call.
return-stops-01.mistake: Do not keep executing a function after it has already returned.

missing-return-01.title: Every path needs a return plan
missing-return-01.body: If one branch returns but another branch reaches the end, the function may hand back no useful value.
missing-return-01.notice: Trace the path for the specific input, not only the branch that looks intended.
missing-return-01.mistake: Do not assume a skipped branch magically returns the other argument.

arg-order-01.title: Arguments fill parameters by position
arg-order-01.body: The first argument goes into the first parameter, the second into the second, and so on unless named arguments are used.
arg-order-01.notice: Write the parameter values before evaluating the body.
arg-order-01.mistake: Do not swap argument meaning because the names would sound nicer the other way.

local-scope-01.title: Local variables stay inside
local-scope-01.body: A value created inside a function or method is not automatically available outside it.
local-scope-01.notice: Use return values to move information out of a function.
local-scope-01.mistake: Do not print an inside-only name after the function has finished.

reuse-01.title: Each call runs fresh
reuse-01.body: Calling the same function more than once applies the same rule to new arguments.
reuse-01.notice: Evaluate each call separately, then combine the returned values.
reuse-01.mistake: Do not reuse the previous call's local parameter values.

function-in-condition-01.title: Boolean functions can drive decisions
function-in-condition-01.body: A function that returns true or false can be used directly as a condition.
function-in-condition-01.notice: Evaluate the returned boolean before choosing the branch.
function-in-condition-01.mistake: Do not print the boolean if the code uses it to choose an if or else path.

param-copy-01.title: Changing a parameter may not change the caller
param-copy-01.body: A parameter is the function's local name for the value it received.
param-copy-01.notice: If the function returns an updated value, the caller must store that return to keep it.
param-copy-01.mistake: Do not assume a local parameter assignment rewrites the original variable.
